title: Typed prefetch + toollet SDK PRD (rough)
content:
Overview:

This is a working PRD sketch for an SDK-and-protocol approach that combines lightweight prefetch hints (client-side), in-band 'toollets' (small proxied tool invocations routed by the hosted API), and typed streaming frames for structured output. Goal: give product teams an ergonomic developer surface that reduces cold tool-call latency, preserves partial structured responses, and exposes telemetry hooks for cost/latency tradeoffs.

Why this matters (motivation):
- Customers building agentic flows complain about latency spikes on first tool call and brittle client-side parsing when a model interleaves text + tool outputs.
- Existing strategies (eager tool call, speculative local exec, full synchronous tool handshake) either increase cost or complicate offline simulation.
- We can improve perceived latency and developer ergonomics by: (a) letting clients signal likely tool usages as cheap "prefetch hints", (b) executing lightweight proxied toollets on behalf of the client in the hosted plane (with strict TTLs and sandboxing), and (c) returning typed, incremental frames that separate human-facing text from structured tool output.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: SDK ergonomics for JS/TS and Python, protocol-level wire framing for streaming responses, telemetry contract (events + tags), and a canary rollout plan behind feature flags.
- Non-goals: supporting full arbitrary customer-run tool code in hosted plane (we keep toollets intentionally limited), replacing on-prem private-deploy tool integrations, or changing billing model right now.

Customer scenarios (concrete):
1) Chat assistant that calls a calendar API on a first user mention. With prefetch hints the SDK primes the calendar token; hosted toollet provides a cached availability check within 40–90ms.
2) Document analysis that invokes a specialized retriever. Typed streaming frames let the client render human explanation first and then commit structured retrieval results when ready.
3) Mobile clients on flaky networks: small prefetch payloads reduce round-trips; progressive frames allow partial UI render and offline resume.

Design principles:
- Bounded surface: prefetch hints are small (max 512 bytes), toollets have explicit capability caps, and typed frames use a compact schema.
- Fail-safe: every toollet must have a fallback (no-op or queued invocation). The model can still emit text-only responses if toollet fails.
- Observable: telemetry emitted for prefetch hit/miss, toollet execution, frame parse errors. Telemetry must include per-request latency tags so cost tradeoffs are visible.
- Ergonomic SDK: simple calls, idiomatic for JS/TS & Python, with default safe behavior and opt-in advanced modes.

Protocol sketch (wire-level):
- Initial call: client sends messages + optional prefetch_hints array of {tool_id, hint_payload, priority_hint}. Hints are advisory, not guaranteed.
- Streaming frames: server emits a stream of frames. Frame types: TEXT_CHUNK, TOOLLET_NOTICE, TOOLLET_RESULT(typed-json), STRUCTURED_COMMIT, META (progress, checksums).
- Typed tool outputs: TOOLLET_RESULT uses a minimal typed envelope: {tool_id, schema_version, payload_type, payload_base64_or_json}. SDK provides helpers to decode and validate against small schemas.

Example flow (pseudo):
1) Client: POST /v1/generate with messages + prefetch_hints:[{tool_id:calendar, hint:"user_mentioned_meeting"}]
2) Server: emits TEXT_CHUNK("Ok, checking availability...")
3) Server: emits TOOLLET_NOTICE({tool_id:calendar, status:"started", trace_id})
4) Server: emits TOOLLET_RESULT({tool_id:calendar, schema_v:1, payload:{availability:[...]} })
5) Server: emits STRUCTURED_COMMIT({bindings:{meeting_suggestion:...}})

SDK ergonomics (JS/TS primary):
- Default: client calls generate() with an optional prefetchHints param. SDK exposes onFrame callbacks: onText, onToolletStart, onToolletResult, onCommit.
- Convenience: decodeTyped(frame) -> typed object or ValidationError. Developers can pass small schema definitions (JSON Schema subset) to verify payloads during dev.
- Backpressure: SDK exposes pause/resume for streaming consumption; default auto-windowing to avoid uncontrolled memory.
- Migration path: existing text-only clients still work; SDK adds opt-in flags to attach prefetch hints and frame handlers.

Toollet sandboxing and safety model:
- Toollets are containerized, short lived, with CPU/memory caps and network egress restrictions.
- Toollet capability manifest: owner registers a declarative manifest for each toollet (allowed endpoints, rate limits). Hosted enforces.
- Billing: toollet execution incurs a small per-call charge; teams can opt-out or route to their Dedicated instance.

Telemetry / observability contract (minimal):
- Events: prefetch_hint_sent, prefetch_hit, prefetch_miss, toollet_start, toollet_done, toollet_error, frame_parse_error, schema_validation_failure.
- Each event includes: request_id, model_id, tool_id (if relevant), latency_ms, outcome enum.
- Console view: per-toollet latency distribution, prefetch efficacy, and per-route structured-commit success rate.

Fallbacks and graceful degradation:
- If a prefetch hint misses: SDK receives prefetch_miss event and the server may launch the toollet on demand (adds ~100–400ms) or queue a background invocation.
- If toollet fails: server emits TOOLLET_RESULT with error envelope; model can choose to synthesize a textual fallback. Client should treat structured output as advisory until a STRUCTURED_COMMIT frame appears.

Security considerations:
- Toollet manifests bound to customer/org; leak risk reduced via egress whitelists and HMAC-signed result envelopes.
- Typed payloads signed when crossing trust boundaries (e.g., shared drives to dedicated customers).

Rollout plan / gating:
- Phase 0 (research): internal experiments with a handful of microtools and JS client test app. Metrics: prefetch hit rate, median toollet latency, frame parse errors. (2–4 weeks)
- Phase 1 (canary): enable behind a flag for 5–10 customers, JS SDK beta. Monitor telemetry & errors. (4–6 weeks)
- Phase 2 (wider beta): add Python SDK ergonomics, opt-in tooling for canary customers. (6–8 weeks)
- Phase 3: default enable with safe heuristics, expose console dashboards and quotas.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Prefetch privacy: what PII can be included in hints? do we need a scrub rule? (action: security review, RFC)
- Toollet chargeback: how granular should per-invocation billing be? (action: finance consult)
- Schema registry: do we build an internal tiny registry for typed envelopes, or piggyback on existing schema infra? (action: infra spike)
- SDK surface area: minimal vs advanced SDK modes — what is default? (product decision)

Next steps (immediate):
- Build a small internal prototype: calendar toollet + retriever toollet + JS minimal SDK. Owner: Claire. Engineers: Ravi, Elliot.
- Open Jira epic INF-3287 with child tasks: toollet-sandbox, frame-protocol, js-sdk-frames, telemetry-pipeline.
- Schedule security review by 2024-11-01.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Could allow negative-priority hints to indicate something is unlikely; useful for batching heuristics.
- Consider a compact binary frame variant for mobile to reduce parse overhead.
- Keep typed payloads small; avoid deep, nested schemas for first iteration.

References and related work:
- internal: confluence:hosted-api/stream-schema-guidelines
- related tickets: INF-3012 (speculative-proxies), INF-3164 (stream-telemetry), SDK PR#214

This is intentionally a rough PRD — goal is to collect feedback from eng + security + infra before formalizing.

-- Claire
